title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock — single pass tracking min price, max profit.
shortTitle: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock — Single Pass

s1_definition.profdef: Given an array of daily prices, the Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock problem finds the maximum profit from one buy followed by one later sell. The single-pass solution tracks the minimum price seen so far and, at each day, computes the profit if you sold that day, which is the current price minus the running minimum, keeping the best such profit. It runs in linear time with constant space, because the buy must come before the sell and the best buy is always the cheapest day seen up to the current day.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh follows a share on the National Bank of India trading app and wants the most he could have made by buying on one day and selling on a later day. Walking through the days once, he remembers the cheapest price he has seen so far. On each new day he asks, "if I had bought at that cheapest earlier price and sold today, how much would I make?" He keeps the biggest such gain. By the last day he knows the best possible single buy-then-sell profit.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track the lowest price so far and the best sell-today-minus-lowest profit in one pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Given an array of daily prices, the Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock problem finds the maximum profit from one buy followed by one later sell. The single-pass solution tracks the minimum price seen so far and, at each day, computes the profit if you sold that day, which is the current price minus the running minimum, keeping the best such profit. It runs in linear time with constant space, because the buy must come before the sell and the best buy is always the cheapest day seen up to the current day.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh follows a share on the National Bank of India trading app and wants the most he could have made by buying on one day and selling on a later day. Walking through the days once, he remembers the cheapest price he has seen so far. On each new day he asks, "if I had bought at that cheapest earlier price and sold today, how much would I make?" He keeps the biggest such gain. By the last day he knows the best possible single buy-then-sell profit.

**One line to remember:** Track the lowest price so far and the best sell-today-minus-lowest profit in one pass.

sections.s2_technical:
The key insight is that for any selling day, the best buying day is the cheapest day at or before it. So you do not need to compare every pair of days; you only need to remember the minimum price seen so far as you move forward. That reduces the naive quadratic double loop to a single linear pass.

You keep two variables. One is the minimum price seen so far, initialised to the first day's price. The other is the best profit seen so far, initialised to zero because doing nothing yields zero profit and you are not forced to trade at a loss. You loop from the second day. On each day you first compute the profit if you sold today, which is today's price minus the running minimum, and update the best profit if that is larger. Then you update the running minimum if today's price is lower. The order is natural: you sell at today's price against the cheapest earlier price, then consider today as a future buy point.

An important design choice is the initial best profit. Starting at zero encodes the rule that you may choose not to trade, so if prices only ever fall the answer is zero rather than a negative loss. If the problem instead required that you must make exactly one transaction even at a loss, you would initialise differently and allow a negative best, so I confirm which variant is being asked.

A senior point is that this classic version allows only one transaction. Variants allow multiple transactions, at most K transactions, or add a cooldown or a fee, and those are solved with dynamic programming, not this simple scan. Recognising which variant you are being asked and not over-engineering the simple one is what an experienced engineer does. I state that this is the single-transaction version.

Another senior point is the data type. For share prices I use BigDecimal to avoid floating-point rounding, comparing with compareTo and subtracting with the BigDecimal subtract method so that fractional currency is exact. I also handle the empty or single-day array by returning zero profit, since you cannot complete a buy and a later sell.

A small finance-domain example: `BigDecimal minPrice = prices[0]; BigDecimal best = BigDecimal.ZERO; for (int i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) { BigDecimal profit = prices[i].subtract(minPrice); if (profit.compareTo(best) > 0) best = profit; if (prices[i].compareTo(minPrice) < 0) minPrice = prices[i]; }` yields the best single-trade profit.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India trading app shows Rajesh a share's daily closing prices and a feature that tells him the best single buy-then-sell profit he could have captured over the window, as an educational backtest. The feature must handle long windows quickly and must never suggest buying after selling. Computing the best one-transaction profit in a single pass is exactly this.

This is exactly how the buy-sell scan works in Java — we track the cheapest price so far and the best sell-today profit.

Problem 2 — Prices are money, so they must be exact BigDecimal values rather than doubles, and the backtest must return zero when the share only ever falls over the window, because Rajesh is not forced to trade at a loss. This shows the money data-type care and the no-forced-loss rule encoded by initialising the best profit to zero.

What the code will do: a `BacktestService` with `maxSingleTradeProfit(BigDecimal[] prices)` tracking running minimum and best profit, returning zero for degenerate windows. The demo backtests a rising-then-falling window and a monotonically falling window.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the rising window prices are `250, 180, 200, 310, 290`.

Step 1: There are five days, enough to trade. minPrice starts at the first day's price `250`, and best starts at zero, encoding that no-trade yields zero.

Step 2: Day index one price `180`. Profit if sold today is `180 - 250 = -70`, which is not greater than best `0`, so best stays zero. Then `180` is less than `250`, so minPrice becomes `180`. We now hold the cheapest buy point.

Step 3: Day index two price `200`. Profit if sold today is `200 - 180 = 20`, which is greater than best `0`, so best becomes `20`. `200` is not less than `180`, so minPrice stays `180`.

Step 4: Day index three price `310`. Profit if sold today is `310 - 180 = 130`, which is greater than best `20`, so best becomes `130`. `310` is not less than `180`, so minPrice stays. This captures the ideal buy at `180` and sell at `310`.

Step 5: Day index four price `290`. Profit if sold today is `290 - 180 = 110`, which is not greater than best `130`, so best stays `130`. The scan ends with best `130`, the maximum single-trade profit, found in one pass without comparing all pairs.

Step 6: For the falling window `400, 350, 300, 250`, every sell-today profit against the running minimum is negative, so best never rises above zero. The method returns zero, correctly encoding that Rajesh should not trade at a loss.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T17:20:00Z INFO Best single-trade profit = Rs.130
2026-10-26T17:20:00Z INFO Rajesh rising-window best profit: Rs.130
2026-10-26T17:20:00Z INFO Best single-trade profit = Rs.0
2026-10-26T17:20:00Z INFO Rajesh falling-window best profit: Rs.0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock asks for the maximum profit from one buy and one later sell, and the single-pass solution tracks two things: the minimum price seen so far and the best profit so far. For each day I first compute the profit if I sold today against the cheapest earlier price and update the best, then I update the running minimum if today is cheaper. Because the best buy for any sell day is the cheapest day up to that point, one linear pass suffices instead of the quadratic all-pairs comparison.

The design choice I always call out is initialising the best profit to zero, which encodes that you are not forced to trade; if prices only fall the answer is zero rather than a loss. If the variant required exactly one transaction even at a loss, I would initialise differently, so I confirm which version is being asked.

I also make clear this is the single-transaction version. Variants that allow multiple transactions, at most K transactions, a cooldown, or a fee are solved with dynamic programming, not this scan, and recognising the variant without over-engineering the simple one is the experienced move. For share prices I use BigDecimal to keep money exact, comparing with compareTo, and I return zero for an empty or single-day window since you cannot buy then sell later.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the trading app's educational backtest, which tells Rajesh the best single buy-then-sell profit he could have captured over a price window, computed quickly even for long windows and never suggesting a buy after a sell. It returns zero when the share only falls, because he is not forced to trade at a loss. Explaining the running-minimum insight, the no-forced-loss encoding, and the variant awareness shows the interviewer that I know the optimal scan and the real trading semantics behind it.
